new_statements.quote: p.4: "We have collected fairly extensive data on three other so-called “Elomwe dialects” in Malawi (Emunyamwelo, Ekokholani, and a variety spoken in Chiradzulu district for which our consultant had no label except “Elomwe”); all of these dialects are highly similar to Emihavani. [...] While the Malawian Elomwe dialects that we have examined do seem to cohere together linguistically (e.g. they share a remarkable suppression of the pitch level of an utterance-final H tone) [...]" p.6: "Emihavani, like all Emakhuwa dialects, has limited lexical tone. [...] Verb stems, on the other hand, do not have any lexical tonal contrasts. Pre-stem elements do have an unpredictable tone pattern, but the macrostem tone shape is entirely a function of the assignment of melodic H tones."
new_statements.citation: Kisseberth, Charles W. & Al Mtenje. 2022. Melodic High tones in Emihavani. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 62(2): 1-33. doi:10.5842/62-2-893
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: statement check: another-languoid-suspected. Opened the mirror text (lines 176-196): the article and the quoted tone statements are about Emihavani, 'the largest dialect of.. Elomwe' in Malawi = Malawi Lomwe [lon] (mala1256); Kokola appears only as 'Ekokholani', one of three other Malawian Elomwe dialects said to be 'highly similar to Emihavani' and to share the suppression of utterance-final H. For Kokola this is at most an inference (tonal, Emakhuwa-type restricted tone), not a statement. | checker: File held by the project (held_mirror koko1267/ +, 34 pp.): title page 'Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus, Vol. 62(2), 2022, 1-33, doi: 10.5842/62-2-893, Melodic High tones in Emihavani,…
new_statements.relation_note: H-tone (H vs toneless) system of the Emakhuwa type: limited lexical tone in nouns, no lexical tone contrast in verb stems, macrostem tone entirely from melodic H assignment rules (MS1, MS2, S3, F, Pen); Emihavani lacks High Tone Doubling and allows word-final H, which is radically suppressed phrase-finally; the examined Malawian Elomwe dialects incl. Ekokholani share that suppression. Nothing on stress/accent.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Restricted ('predictable') Bantu tone system: H tones assigned by rule to macrostem moras (first, second, third-of-stem, final or penultimate mora depending on tense); nouns with limited lexical tone; no word-stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: Chichewa loans give nouns some tonal unpredictability; phrase-final H radically suppressed except in yes-no questions; a few H deletions/assignments outside the melodic system
new_statements.identity_note: Ekokholani = Kokhola/Kokola [kzn]: Ethnologue kzn 'Alternate Names Kokhola.. Thyolo district: Sandama area' and Kalinde 2018 locates Ekokholani speakers at Sandama, Thekelani, Khonjeni, Goliati, Thyolo. The detailed tonal analysis is of Emihavani (Malawi Lomwe [lon], mala1256); Ekokholani is explicitly named (p.4) as a dialect on which the authors collected 'fairly extensive data', 'highly similar to Emihavani', and included among 'the Malawian Elomwe dialects that we have examined' sharing the utterance-final H-tone suppression; the p.6 sentence is a group-level statement ('like all Emakhuwa dialects') under which the authors subsume Malawian Elomwe. Partly group-level statement. [name in source: Ekokholani (one of four 'Malawian Elomwe' dialects; main object of study is Emihavani); pages 3-7 (esp. p.4, p.6)]
